claims.text: The nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially form a uniform solid solution.
Structural and chemical stability across 473–1923 K is governed by high configurational entropy.
High configurational entropy stabilizes a disordered solid solution.
High configurational entropy induces local lattice-strain fields.
High configurational entropy reduces the thermodynamic driving force for phase segregation.
High configurational entropy suppresses diffusion and slows atomic mobility.
Reduced atomic mobility kinetically limits phase segregation and chemical rearrangement during thermal cycling.
The proposed intervention is thermal cycling from 473 K to 1923 K under an inert atmosphere.
An inert atmosphere minimizes oxidation and other reactive degradation.
Adequate dwell times permit atomic rearrangement when it is not kinetically hindered.
After thermal cycling, the nanoparticles will retain a single-phase structure relative to the initial state.
After thermal cycling, the nanoparticles will remain chemically homogeneous with minimal elemental segregation relative to the initial state.
The predicted stability is limited to controlled inert atmospheres and temperatures within 473–1923 K.
Reactive atmospheres or temperatures outside 473–1923 K may activate alternative degradation pathways.
Partial ordering can be used to produce a lower-configurational-entropy control.
Comparable or greater segregation, chemical inhomogeneity, or secondary-phase formation in the high-entropy sample than in the low-entropy control would falsify the hypothesis.
